To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) past-tense generation is more difficult when the stem is not provided, (b) past-tense production is more difficult when it is based on a picture of the verb's meaning than when it is based upon the verb's stem, (c) the model we present is consistent with these findings and (d) the model is consistent with a number of other findings that are not discussed in this abstract.

(a) a robust regularity effect in past tense generation from form is no longer reliable when the task involves generation from meaning; (b) this outcome would appear problematic to the extent that dual-mechanism models of inflection assume the process of stem retrieval is obligatory; and (c) by contrast, it supports models that consider stem-retrieval to be task-dependent.
(1) the standard form task is not the best way to test dual-mechanism models and (2) a single-mechanical model of verb inflecting can account for the data.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the nature of the mental processes involved in the production of regular and irregular verb forms and with the role played by the task in which the participant is involved.
the nature of the relationship between the representation of meaning and the representation of form.
the nature of inflectional processing and its neural basis, and with the role of semantics in the processing of regular and irregular verbs.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the dual-mechanism theory is not supported by our data, and that the single-mechanism theory, at least in its current form, is not supported either.
the results of the present experiment support single-mechanism accounts of past-tense generation, but that they do not rule out dual-mechanism models.
the dual-mechanism theory is not falsified and the single-mechanism theory has not been proven.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the task used to investigate verb inflection has a significant impact on the pattern of results.
the task used to study verb morphology can influence the pattern of results obtained.
the dual mechanism model can account for the data from the standard form condition but not the data from the picture condition.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the regularity effect observed when participants generate the past tense of verbs from the stem can be accounted for in terms of a single mechanism, but this is not necessarily the case when the task requires participants to generate the past form of a verb from meaning.

a single-mechanic model of verb inflecton that incorporates distributed phonological and meaning representations can account for the pattern of data obtained from the standard and meaning generation task.
a model that can account for the data from the standard task can be used to make predictions about the data from the new task.
